stimuli.title: Federalist No. 51, 1788 (adapted excerpt)
stimuli.text: But what is government itself, but the greatest of all reflections on human nature? If men were angels, no government would be necessary. If angels were to govern men, neither external nor internal controls on government would be necessary. In framing a government which is to be administered by men over men, the great difficulty lies in this: you must first enable the government to control the governed; and in the next place oblige it to control itself. ... Ambition must be made to counteract ambition.

stimuli.title: Brutus No. 1, 1787 (adapted excerpt)
stimuli.text: In a republic, the manners, sentiments, and interests of the people should be similar. If this be not the case, there will be a constant clashing of opinions; and the representatives of one part will be continually striving against those of the other. ... The legislature under this constitution may pass any law which they may think necessary and proper to carry into effect the powers given them. ... A free republic cannot succeed over a country of such immense extent as that of the whole United States.

stimuli.title: Federalist No. 39, 1788 (adapted excerpt)
stimuli.text: The proposed Constitution, therefore, is, in strictness, neither a national nor a federal Constitution, but a composition of both. In its foundation it is federal, not national; in the sources from which its ordinary powers are drawn, it is partly federal and partly national; in the operation of these powers, it is national, not federal; in the extent of them, again, it is federal, not national; and, finally, in the authoritative mode of introducing amendments, it is neither wholly federal nor wholly national.

stimuli.title: Federalist No. 70, 1788 (adapted excerpt)
stimuli.text: Energy in the executive is a leading character in the definition of good government. ... The ingredients which constitute energy in the executive are, first, unity; secondly, duration; thirdly, an adequate provision for its support; fourthly, competent powers. ... Decision, activity, secrecy, and dispatch will generally characterize the proceedings of one man in a much more eminent degree than the proceedings of any greater number.

stimuli.title: Federalist No. 78, 1788 (adapted excerpt)
stimuli.text: Whoever attentively considers the different departments of power must perceive, that, in a government in which they are separated from each other, the judiciary, from the nature of its functions, will always be the least dangerous to the political rights of the Constitution. ... It may truly be said to have neither FORCE nor WILL, but merely judgment. ... The interpretation of the laws is the proper and peculiar province of the courts.

stimuli.title: A high school newspaper editorial (practice text)
stimuli.text: Last week three students were suspended for wearing T-shirts with a slogan opposing the city's new youth curfew. Not one class was interrupted. Nobody shouted, and no teacher had to stop a lesson. We did not give up our rights when we walked through the front doors of this building. If a public school can punish quiet political expression, it is teaching us that the Constitution ends at the parking lot.

stimuli.title: A political scientist's overview (practice text)
stimuli.text: For most of American history, the Bill of Rights limited only the national government. The change came case by case. Over the twentieth century, the Supreme Court used the due process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment to apply most of the protections in the Bill of Rights to the states, one right at a time. A few protections, such as the right to be indicted by a grand jury, still bind only the federal government.

stimuli.title: Emancipation Proclamation, 1863 (adapted excerpt)
stimuli.text: All persons held as slaves within any State or designated part of a State, the people whereof shall then be in rebellion against the United States, shall be then, thenceforward, and forever free; and the Executive Government of the United States, including the military and naval authority thereof, will recognize and maintain the freedom of such persons.

stimuli.title: A campaign manager's memo (practice text)
stimuli.text: We cannot win this district on television ads alone. Our data team has matched the voter file with consumer records, so we know which households care most about school funding and which care most about property taxes. Each group will get its own message: text messages, targeted online ads and volunteers at the door. Small online donations from supporters will carry us to the final week, and we will not depend on the state party.

questions.stem: The author's main argument is that
options: a government must be built to restrain itself
government is unneeded in a virtuous republic
every federal official should be elected directly
a strong executive is the best cure for faction
questions.explanation: Madison says the government must first control the governed and then be obliged to control itself, which the Constitution does through separate branches that check one another.

questions.stem: Which feature of the Constitution best reflects the idea that "ambition must be made to counteract ambition"?
options: The method of amending the Constitution in Article V
Equal representation of the states in the Senate
The ban on religious tests for federal office
The House's power to impeach executive officers
questions.explanation: Impeachment gives one branch a weapon against officials of another, so each branch's ambition guards against the others. Equal Senate seats concern federalism, not checks between branches.

questions.stem: Which change would the author most likely see as a threat to the principle in the excerpt?
options: A president who vetoes many bills
A legislature able to remove judges at will
Senators chosen directly by the voters
A state adding rights to its own constitution
questions.explanation: If the legislature could remove judges whenever it liked, the courts could no longer check it, and power would gather in one branch. Frequent vetoes are the checks working as designed.

questions.stem: The author of Brutus No. 1 would most likely respond to the excerpt that
options: a strong president is the best check on Congress
a large republic will still drift toward tyranny
the national government should control the states
separated branches make the states unnecessary
questions.explanation: Brutus argued that no free republic could govern so large a country and that the new national government would swallow the states, whatever its internal checks.

questions.stem: Under the Articles of Confederation, a change to the Articles required
options: approval by nine of the thirteen states
questions.explanation: Amendments needed the consent of all thirteen state legislatures, so a single state could block any reform. Nine states were needed only to pass major laws.

questions.stem: A state law conflicts with a valid federal statute on the same subject. Which part of the Constitution settles the conflict?
options: The full faith and credit clause
questions.explanation: The supremacy clause in Article VI makes the Constitution and federal laws made under it the supreme law of the land, so the valid federal statute prevails.

questions.stem: A city lets residents vote directly on how to spend part of its budget. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Participatory democracy stresses broad, direct involvement of citizens in decisions. Pluralist democracy works through competing groups, and elite democracy through a small, educated few.

questions.stem: Congress gives states highway money only if they set the drinking age at 21. This is an example of
options: a block grant states may spend freely
an unfunded mandate on the states
a power the Constitution reserves to states
questions.explanation: The money is for a specific purpose and comes with a condition attached, the mark of a categorical grant. A block grant gives broad discretion, and an unfunded mandate gives no money at all.

questions.stem: Which is an exclusive power of the national government?
questions.explanation: Article I gives Congress the power to coin money and Article I, Section 10 forbids the states to do it. Taxing, borrowing and setting up courts are concurrent powers.

questions.stem: A state puts a special tax only on the branch of a federally chartered bank inside its borders. Which required case most directly supports striking the tax down?
questions.explanation: In McCulloch the Court held that Congress could charter a bank under the necessary and proper clause and that a state could not tax it, since federal law is supreme over state law.

questions.stem: According to the table, about what percent of House bills introduced were enacted into law?
questions.explanation: 200 enacted out of 8,000 introduced is 200 / 8,000 = 2.5%. The 33% figure divides by the 600 bills that passed the House, not by all bills introduced.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: Most bills that pass a chamber become law
Senate committees report most of their bills
The Senate enacts more bills than the House
questions.explanation: Only 700 of 8,000 House bills and 450 of 4,500 Senate bills were reported out of committee, about 9 to 10 percent. Of bills that passed a chamber, only about a third became law.

questions.stem: Which feature of Congress best explains the pattern in the table?
options: Courts strike down most new laws
questions.explanation: Standing committees decide which bills get hearings and markup, and most bills die there without action. The filibuster exists only in the Senate, and vetoes are rare.

questions.stem: Which concept does the infographic illustrate?
options: Checks Congress places on the president
Formal powers listed in Article I
Powers the president shares with governors
questions.explanation: Executive orders, executive agreements and signing statements are not spelled out in the Constitution; presidents use them as informal powers to act without Congress.

questions.stem: Which action could Congress take to limit the use of a power shown in the infographic?
options: Remove the president by majority vote
Veto the executive order by majority vote
Ask the Supreme Court for an advisory opinion
Deny funding for carrying out an order
questions.explanation: Congress controls appropriations, so it can refuse to fund what an order directs. Congress has no veto over the president, removal needs a two-thirds Senate vote after impeachment, and federal courts give no advisory opinions.

questions.stem: A senator follows her constituents' wishes on local issues but her own judgment on foreign policy. She is acting under the
questions.explanation: The politico model blends the delegate and trustee roles, following constituents on some issues and personal judgment on others.

questions.stem: In the Senate, ending a filibuster on most legislation requires
options: approval from the Senate Rules Committee
a cloture vote of three-fifths of senators
a two-thirds vote of senators present
a simple majority of senators present and voting
questions.explanation: Under Senate Rule XXII, cloture on most legislation needs three-fifths of the senators duly chosen and sworn, which is 60 of 100.

questions.stem: Which body in the House sets the terms of debate and amendment for most major bills?
questions.explanation: The House Rules Committee writes a rule for each major bill setting debate time and which amendments may be offered. Ways and Means handles taxes.

questions.stem: A president uses the bully pulpit by
questions.explanation: The bully pulpit is the president's ability to speak to the nation and rally public opinion to pressure Congress.

questions.stem: About what percent of the petitions filed did the Court agree to hear?
questions.explanation: 60 granted out of 4,000 filed is 60 / 4,000 = 0.015, or 1.5%. Moving the decimal one place too far gives 15%.

questions.stem: Which practice explains how the Court decides which petitions in the table to grant?
options: A majority vote of the justices
A two-thirds vote of the justices
questions.explanation: The Court grants certiorari when at least four of the nine justices vote to hear a case. The solicitor general argues for the government but does not decide.

questions.stem: In Marbury v. Madison (1803), the Court ruled that part of the Judiciary Act of 1789 was unconstitutional. The case matters today because it
options: gave Congress power over the Court's size
required the Senate to confirm all judges
let courts strike down acts of Congress
questions.explanation: By refusing to apply a section of a federal law that conflicted with the Constitution, the Court established its power to declare acts of the other branches void.

questions.stem: When the Court relies on its own earlier decisions to decide a similar new case, it is following
questions.explanation: Stare decisis ("let the decision stand") means following precedent so that the law stays stable and predictable.

questions.stem: A justice who believes courts should defer to elected branches unless a law clearly breaks the Constitution favors
questions.explanation: Judicial restraint asks judges to uphold laws passed by elected officials unless they plainly violate the Constitution. Judicial activism is more willing to strike laws down or set policy.

questions.stem: Which is a way Congress can check the federal courts?
options: Overturning a constitutional ruling by vote
Vetoing a decision of the Court
questions.explanation: Article III lets Congress make exceptions to the Court's appellate jurisdiction. A constitutional ruling can be undone only by amendment or a later ruling, and impeachment is for misconduct, not decisions.

questions.stem: Close, lasting ties among a congressional committee, a federal agency and an interest group are called
questions.explanation: In an iron triangle the committee funds the agency, the agency serves the group, and the group supports the committee members, so all three gain.

questions.stem: Congress passes a law requiring "safe" drinking water, and the Environmental Protection Agency sets the exact limit for each chemical. This shows
questions.explanation: Congress often writes laws in general terms and leaves agencies to fill in the details by issuing rules, which gives the bureaucracy real policy-making power.

questions.stem: The editorial's argument is most directly supported by
questions.explanation: In Tinker the Court held that public school students wearing black armbands to protest the Vietnam War were protected by the First Amendment's free speech clause.

questions.stem: Under the precedent the editors rely on, the school could most likely punish the shirts if it showed that
options: the city council objected to them
their message was about a political issue
questions.explanation: Tinker allows schools to limit student expression that would materially and substantially disrupt the school. Dislike of a political message is not enough.

questions.stem: The First Amendment limits a public school, a body of state government, because the Supreme Court has
options: ruled that public schools are federal agencies
used the supremacy clause against state laws
applied the Tenth Amendment to every public school
incorporated it through the Fourteenth Amendment
questions.explanation: Through selective incorporation, the Court has used the Fourteenth Amendment's due process clause to apply the First Amendment's protections to state and local governments.

questions.stem: A public school district begins each day with a short nondenominational prayer led by teachers, though students may stay silent. Which required case shows the policy is unconstitutional?
questions.explanation: Engel held that school-sponsored prayer violates the establishment clause even when it is nondenominational and students may decline to take part.

questions.stem: A man charged with a felony in state court cannot afford a lawyer, and the judge refuses to appoint one. Which required case protects him?
options: New York Times Co. v. United States
questions.explanation: Gideon held that the Sixth Amendment right to counsel applies to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment, so states must provide lawyers to poor felony defendants.

questions.stem: Police must warn a suspect in custody of the right to remain silent before questioning. The warning protects a right in the
questions.explanation: The Miranda warnings protect the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination. The Eighth Amendment concerns bail and punishment.

questions.stem: Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 prohibits
options: religious tests for any federal or state office
sex discrimination in federally funded schools
questions.explanation: Title IX bars discrimination on the basis of sex in education programs that receive federal money, and it greatly expanded girls' and women's school sports.

questions.stem: In "Letter from a Birmingham Jail," Martin Luther King, Jr. argues that people have a moral duty to
options: use force against officials who break the law
disobey unjust laws openly and peacefully
leave civil rights to the federal courts
obey every law until a court strikes it down
questions.explanation: King defends nonviolent civil disobedience: breaking an unjust law in the open, without violence and accepting the penalty, rather than waiting for change.

questions.stem: Amish parents refuse to keep their children in school past eighth grade, citing their faith, and the state fines them. Which required case supports the parents?
questions.explanation: Yoder held that requiring Amish children to attend school beyond eighth grade violates the free exercise clause. Engel concerned the establishment clause.

questions.stem: Which statement is supported by the data?
options: Support for bigger government falls with age
Every age group prefers smaller government
Views on government do not differ by age
Most adults over 50 want a bigger government
questions.explanation: Support for a bigger government drops steadily from 62% among 18-29 year olds to 38% among those 65 and older, while support for a smaller government rises.

questions.stem: By how many percentage points does support for a bigger government among 18-29 year olds exceed that among adults 65 and older?
questions.explanation: 62 - 38 = 24 points. Comparing the smaller-government column (59 - 36) gives 23, and mixing columns (62 - 36) gives 26.

questions.stem: A pollster wants a survey like this one to reflect all adults. The most important step is
options: asking questions in a leading way
questions.explanation: In a random sample every adult has an equal chance of being chosen, so the sample mirrors the population. Self-selected samples over-represent people with strong views.

questions.stem: A candidate promises to lower taxes and reduce government regulation of business. This platform is most consistent with
questions.explanation: Conservatives generally favor lower taxes, less regulation and a smaller role for government in the economy.

questions.stem: The Federal Reserve raises interest rates to slow inflation. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Monetary policy is the Federal Reserve's control of the money supply and interest rates. Fiscal policy is taxing and spending by Congress and the president.

questions.stem: A poll asks, "Do you support the reckless plan to cut school funding?" The main problem with the poll is that
options: the margin of error is too small
questions.explanation: The word "reckless" pushes respondents toward one answer, so the results measure the wording as much as opinion.

questions.stem: Which is usually the most important early agent of political socialization?
questions.explanation: Children first learn political attitudes and often party loyalty at home; schools, peers and media add to them later.

questions.stem: Which age group's turnout fell the most from the presidential election to the midterm election?
questions.explanation: Turnout among 18-24 year olds fell 20 points (48 to 28), compared with 18, 13 and 8 points for the older groups.

questions.stem: Which reform would most likely raise turnout among the youngest voters in the table?
options: Moving all elections to midterm years
questions.explanation: Young people move often and are least likely to be registered, so letting them register and vote on the same day removes a key barrier. The table shows midterms have lower turnout.

questions.stem: The note on the map describes
questions.explanation: Giving all of a state's electoral votes to the candidate with the most popular votes there is the winner-take-all system. Maine and Nebraska instead award some votes by district.

questions.stem: Because of the system in the note, presidential candidates tend to
options: need a majority of the national vote
spend most time in the safest states
questions.explanation: A narrow win in a closely divided state earns all its electoral votes, so campaigns pour time and money into swing states. A candidate can win without a national popular majority.

questions.stem: Third parties rarely win seats in Congress mainly because of
options: federal limits on how large a party may be
the Electoral College's role in House races
a constitutional ban on third parties
questions.explanation: When one candidate wins each district with the most votes, a third party with steady but small support wins nothing, so voters drift to the two major parties.

questions.stem: A voter picks the candidate whose tax plan will most help her own family's budget. This is
questions.explanation: Rational-choice voting is based on what the voter judges to be in her own interest. Retrospective voting judges past performance.

questions.stem: The cartoon's main message is that
options: members of Congress ignore rich donors
voters give too much money to campaigns
lobbying has been banned by federal law
big donors drown out ordinary voters
questions.explanation: The money piled on the desk and the lobbyist at the member's ear, with voters held behind a rope, suggest that wealthy interests get access that ordinary citizens do not.

questions.stem: Which required case most directly opened the way for the kind of spending shown in the cartoon?
options: New York Times Co. v. United States
questions.explanation: Citizens United held that independent political spending by corporations, associations and unions is protected speech, which led to super PACs that may raise and spend without limit.

questions.stem: Which statement is supported by the table?
options: Fewer than half of incumbents in either house won
House incumbents won more often than Senate ones
Reelection rates rose in every election
questions.explanation: House rates (93 to 97%) were above Senate rates (79 to 91%) in every election. Senate rates were never 100%, and both fell in Election 2.

questions.stem: Which best explains the high rates for House incumbents?
options: Ballots that do not list any party
Term limits on members of the House
House elections held every six years
questions.explanation: Incumbents are better known, raise more money, do casework for constituents and often run in districts drawn to favor their party. There are no congressional term limits.

questions.stem: Many people enjoy the benefits an interest group wins without joining or paying dues. This is
questions.explanation: Because the benefits go to everyone, people have an incentive to let others pay, which makes it hard for groups to recruit members.

questions.stem: News coverage focused on who is ahead in the polls rather than on candidates' policies is called
questions.explanation: Horse-race journalism treats a campaign like a race, stressing poll standings and strategy over issues.

questions.stem: The author's main concern is that
options: small republics fall to majority factions
a large republic cannot represent its people well
the states will keep too much power over foreign trade
questions.explanation: Brutus argues that people across so wide a country have different interests, so their representatives will clash and a free republic cannot work at that size.

questions.stem: The author's warning about laws "necessary and proper" to carry out federal powers anticipated the debate later decided in
options: New York Times Co. v. United States
questions.explanation: McCulloch read the necessary and proper clause broadly, upholding a national bank as an implied power, the very expansion Brutus feared.

questions.stem: Madison answered arguments like this one in Federalist No. 10 by claiming that a large republic
options: lets the states keep their own armed militias
makes it harder for one faction to dominate
gives each citizen a direct vote on laws
questions.explanation: Madison argued that a large republic takes in so many interests that no single faction is likely to form a majority and oppress the rest. He thought the causes of faction could not be removed.

questions.stem: Which part of the Constitution was added in part to answer fears like the author's about distant national power?
questions.explanation: The Tenth Amendment, part of the Bill of Rights demanded by Anti-Federalists, reserves to the states or the people the powers not delegated to the national government.

questions.stem: The Declaration of Independence says people may "alter or abolish" a government that destroys their rights. This idea reflects
questions.explanation: Social contract theory holds that government exists by agreement of the people to protect their rights, so a government that breaks the agreement loses its claim to obedience.

questions.stem: Which step that Article V allows has never been used to add an amendment to the Constitution?
options: Ratification by conventions in three-fourths of the states
Proposal by a two-thirds vote in both houses of Congress
Proposal by a convention called by two-thirds of the states
Ratification by three-fourths of the state legislatures
questions.explanation: Every amendment so far was proposed by Congress, never by a convention called on the application of two-thirds of the state legislatures. Most were ratified by state legislatures, and the Twenty-first Amendment was ratified by state conventions.

questions.stem: A federal law requires states to make polling places accessible to voters with disabilities but gives no money to do it. This is
questions.explanation: A mandate is a federal requirement on the states; when it comes without money to pay for it, it is unfunded. Both kinds of grant send money.

questions.stem: Congress makes it a federal crime to carry a knife near any public park, citing its power over interstate commerce. Which required case would opponents cite?
questions.explanation: In Lopez the Court held that carrying a gun near a school was not economic activity substantially affecting interstate commerce, so Congress had exceeded its commerce power.

questions.stem: Since the 1990s, Congress has given states more control over some programs, such as welfare, through block grants. This trend is called
questions.explanation: Devolution shifts responsibility from the national government back to the states. Preemption is the opposite, federal law displacing state law.

questions.stem: The course lists the Gettysburg Address, given during the Civil War, among the foundational documents mainly because it
options: explained the Supreme Court's role in the war
set out the president's war powers in law
reaffirmed equality and government by the people
ended slavery in the states loyal to the Union
questions.explanation: The College Board framework says the address reaffirmed equality and popular sovereignty as foundations of American democracy. It was a speech, not a law, and it freed no one.

questions.stem: Which president had the highest share of regular vetoes overridden?
questions.explanation: President B had 6 of 30 overridden (20%), President D 4 of 25 (16%), President C 1 of 12 (about 8%) and President A none.

questions.stem: Which conclusion do the veto data best support?
options: Most vetoes are overridden by Congress
Overrides are most common under unified government
Presidents veto more when their party controls Congress
Vetoes are more common under divided government
questions.explanation: The two presidents facing a Congress of the other party issued 30 and 25 vetoes; the one with his own party in control issued 2. Overrides were a small share for everyone.

questions.stem: Near the end of a session, a president facing a Congress like President B's wants to block a bill without risking an override. The president could use
questions.explanation: If Congress adjourns within ten days (Sundays excepted) of sending a bill and the president does not sign it, the bill dies and cannot be overridden. The line-item veto was struck down in 1998.

questions.stem: The cartoonist's main point is that
options: Congress now controls the executive branch
presidents have taken power from Congress
the courts have weakened the presidency
questions.explanation: The towering executive holding orders and declarations next to a tiny Congress with a sign reading "Article I" suggests the president now exercises powers the Constitution gave to Congress.

questions.stem: Which argument from the foundational documents could be used to defend the executive in the cartoon?
options: Factions are best controlled in a large republic
The judiciary is the least dangerous branch
Energy in the executive aids good government
A free republic needs a small territory
questions.explanation: Federalist No. 70 argues that a single, energetic executive acts with decision and dispatch, which supporters of strong presidential power often cite.

questions.stem: Gridlock in Washington is most likely when
options: the president signs most bills sent to the desk
different parties hold Congress and the presidency
one party holds the presidency and both chambers of Congress
the House and Senate pass identical bills quickly
questions.explanation: Divided government gives each party a check on the other, so bills stall more often than when one party controls both branches.

questions.stem: The House of Representatives has the sole power to
questions.explanation: The House impeaches (brings charges) by majority vote; the Senate holds the trial. Confirmations and treaty approval belong to the Senate.

questions.stem: Two members of Congress agree to vote for each other's bills. This practice is
questions.explanation: Logrolling is vote trading. Pork barrel spending is money directed to a member's district.

questions.stem: Which presidential power is a formal power stated in Article II?
questions.explanation: Article II gives the president power to grant reprieves and pardons for federal offenses. The other three are informal powers developed through practice.

questions.stem: What percent of nominees were confirmed when the other party held the Senate majority?
questions.explanation: 48 of 80 is 60%. 90% is the rate under a Senate of the president's party, 75% is the overall rate (120 of 160), and 40% is the share not confirmed.

questions.stem: Which constitutional feature best explains the difference shown in the table?
options: The Senate's power to confirm judges
The president's power to remove judges
The courts' power of judicial review
The House's role in approving nominees
questions.explanation: Judges are appointed with the advice and consent of the Senate, so a Senate majority from the other party can slow or block nominees. Presidents cannot remove federal judges, and the House has no role.

questions.stem: Voters in a fast-growing city sue because their state has not redrawn legislative districts in sixty years, so their votes count for far less than rural votes. Which required case lets federal courts hear the claim?
questions.explanation: Baker v. Carr held that apportionment is not a political question beyond the courts, so voters may challenge unequal districts under the equal protection clause. Shaw v. Reno concerned race-based districting.

questions.stem: Because federal courts have no army and no budget of their own, their power depends most on
options: approval by the attorney general's office
a yearly review by the House
questions.explanation: Courts must rely on the other branches to enforce rulings, so their legitimacy, the public's belief that their decisions are proper, is their main source of power.

questions.stem: A congressional committee holds hearings at which agency heads explain how they spent their funds. This is
questions.explanation: Oversight is Congress's review of how the executive branch carries out the laws, through hearings, investigations and control of funding.

questions.stem: Federal civil servants may not take part in partisan political activity while on duty. This limit comes from
options: the Budget and Impoundment Control Act
questions.explanation: The Hatch Act restricts the partisan political activity of federal employees to keep the civil service neutral. The Freedom of Information Act opens agency records to the public.

questions.stem: Most cases reach the Supreme Court through
questions.explanation: Nearly all of the Court's cases are appeals from lower federal courts or state supreme courts. Original jurisdiction covers only a few cases, such as disputes between states.

questions.stem: A critic says the Court is "legislating from the bench" when it strikes down a popular law. The critic objects to
questions.explanation: The charge of legislating from the bench is a criticism of judicial activism, judges using rulings to make policy that critics think belongs to elected branches.

questions.stem: The process the author describes is known as
questions.explanation: Selective incorporation is the case-by-case application of Bill of Rights protections to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment's due process clause.

questions.stem: Which required case is an example of the process in the passage?
questions.explanation: McDonald held that the Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms for self-defense applies to the states, incorporating it through the Fourteenth Amendment.

questions.stem: According to the author, before the change described the Bill of Rights
options: had never been tested in court
applied only to the state governments
questions.explanation: The passage says that for most of American history the Bill of Rights limited only the national government, until the Court began applying it to the states.

questions.stem: A newspaper obtains a secret government study of a war, and the government asks a court to stop publication. Which required case most supports the newspaper?
options: New York Times Co. v. United States
Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission
questions.explanation: In the Pentagon Papers case the Court ruled that the government had not met the heavy burden required for prior restraint, even with national security claims.

questions.stem: A state draws a congressional district shaped only to gather voters of one race, with no other explanation. Under which required case can voters challenge it?
questions.explanation: Shaw v. Reno held that a district drawn with race as the only factor can be challenged under the equal protection clause. Baker v. Carr concerned unequal population.

questions.stem: A state law forbids a church to use wine in its religious services. The church would most likely argue that the law violates
options: the full faith and credit clause
questions.explanation: A law that burdens the practice of a religion raises a free exercise claim. The establishment clause bars government support for religion.

questions.stem: Supreme Court debate over affirmative action in admissions has centered on
options: the First Amendment's free exercise clause
questions.explanation: The cases ask whether considering race or other characteristics in admissions is consistent with the Fourteenth Amendment's guarantee of equal protection of the laws.

questions.stem: In Griswold v. Connecticut (1965), the Court recognized a right to privacy that it found
options: created by an act of Congress
questions.explanation: The Constitution never names a right to privacy; the Court reasoned that it is implied by several Bill of Rights guarantees and protected by due process.

questions.stem: A prison sentence far out of proportion to a minor crime would most likely be challenged under the
questions.explanation: The Eighth Amendment forbids cruel and unusual punishments and excessive bail and fines.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the poll?
options: Democrats are evenly divided on it
Independents strongly oppose the new policy
Views on the policy split sharply by party
questions.explanation: 78% of Democrats support it while 75% of Republicans oppose it, a wide partisan gap. Independents are close to even.

questions.stem: Given the margin of error, the result for all adults is best described as
options: too close to call with confidence
proof that the policy will pass Congress
questions.explanation: Support could be as low as 48% and opposition as high as 49%, so the ranges overlap and the poll cannot say which side has a majority.

questions.stem: The pattern among party members in the poll is an example of
questions.explanation: Polarization means the parties' members hold increasingly opposite views, as the 78 to 22 split shows.

questions.stem: A voter wants the government to stay out of both the economy and people's personal choices. This view is best called
questions.explanation: Libertarians favor minimal government in both economic and social life. Liberals tend to favor more economic regulation, and conservatives more social regulation.

questions.stem: During a recession, Congress increases spending and cuts taxes to boost demand. This approach reflects
questions.explanation: Keynesian theory holds that government should raise demand in a downturn through spending and tax cuts, even with deficits. Laissez-faire means leaving the economy alone.

questions.stem: Surveys of voters taken as they leave polling places on Election Day are
questions.explanation: Exit polls question voters right after they vote. Tracking polls follow opinion over a campaign, and push polls are campaign tactics disguised as surveys.

questions.stem: A court orders a governor to obey a state law just as any other resident must. This reflects the core value of
questions.explanation: The course lists the rule of law among core American values: no one, however powerful, is above the law.

questions.stem: Which trend does the table show?
options: A growing share of adults call themselves independent
The Democratic share grows over the thirty years
The shares of all three groups stay roughly the same over time
A growing share of adults call themselves Republican
questions.explanation: Independents rise from 33% to 42% over thirty years while both major parties' shares fall.

questions.stem: The trend in the table is most consistent with
questions.explanation: Dealignment is a decline in attachment to either party. A realignment would shift lasting support from one party to the other.

questions.stem: Compared with the period before the 1970s, the process in the infographic gives
options: voters, not party leaders, the main say
party leaders more control over nominees
Congress a role in naming nominees
caucuses in place of every primary
questions.explanation: Reforms after 1968 tied delegates to primary and caucus results, so voters rather than party bosses at conventions now largely choose nominees.

questions.stem: States that move their contests in Step 1 earlier to gain influence are
questions.explanation: Front-loading is scheduling primaries and caucuses early in the season, when they can shape which candidates survive.

questions.stem: The National Voter Registration Act of 1993 made it easier to vote by
options: allowing online voting in all federal races
mailing every adult a ballot automatically
letting people register at motor vehicle offices
making Election Day a paid holiday in every state
questions.explanation: Known as the motor voter law, it required states to offer voter registration when people apply for or renew a driver's license, and by mail.

questions.stem: Voters who punish the president's party because the economy did poorly over the past year are
questions.explanation: Retrospective voting judges candidates or parties by past results. Prospective voting judges them by promises for the future.

questions.stem: The infographic shows
options: a decline in social media use
a steady rise in trust in printed newspapers
a shift from traditional to digital news
questions.explanation: Television and print fall while social media and news websites become the largest source, a move from traditional to digital media.

questions.stem: One concern raised by the trend in the infographic is that
options: the government will take over running the newspapers
people may see mostly news that fits their views
news will become impossible to find
questions.explanation: Social media feeds tailor content to users, so people can end up in echo chambers that reinforce their views and spread unverified stories.

questions.stem: Compared with the challenger, the incumbent relied more on money from
questions.explanation: PACs gave 40% of the incumbent's money but only 10% of the challenger's. The challenger relied more on individual donors and personal money.

questions.stem: Which best explains why PACs give more to incumbents than to challengers?
options: PACs may give only to incumbents
Challengers may not accept PAC money
questions.explanation: PACs seek access to the officials who will vote on their issues, and incumbents are very likely to be in office after the election.

questions.stem: A former member of Congress becomes a lobbyist for firms her committee once oversaw. Critics call this
questions.explanation: The revolving door is the movement of people between government jobs and the industries or groups they deal with.

questions.stem: An interest group rates members of Congress on key votes and publishes the scores. The main aim of this tactic is to
options: file briefs in Supreme Court cases
questions.explanation: Scorecards tell members' voters how they voted on the group's issues, which pressures members to vote the group's way.

questions.stem: The author's main claim is that the Constitution
options: keeps the Articles' league of states
lets each state veto federal laws
questions.explanation: Madison calls the plan "neither a national nor a federal Constitution, but a composition of both": some parts rest on the states and some on the people as a whole.

questions.stem: Which feature of the Constitution is "federal" in the author's sense because it treats the states as equals?
options: Equal state votes in the Senate
questions.explanation: In Federalist No. 39, "federal" means resting on the states as equal political bodies. Equal Senate representation does that; House seats by population rest on the people.

questions.stem: In saying the powers "operate" nationally, the author means that federal laws
options: must first be approved by each state legislature
are enforced only by state courts
questions.explanation: Under the Articles, Congress acted on the states; under the Constitution, federal laws reach individuals directly. The extent of the powers is limited, which Madison calls federal.

questions.stem: A political scientist argues that a small, wealthy and educated group shapes most policy decisions. This view reflects
questions.explanation: The elite model holds that a limited, highly educated or wealthy few hold most influence. The pluralist model sees many competing groups.

questions.stem: Farm, labor and business organizations each press Congress, and policy reflects bargaining among them. This best fits
questions.explanation: Pluralist democracy sees policy as the result of competition and compromise among many organized groups.

questions.stem: Which weakness of the Articles of Confederation did the Constitution address by creating a national executive?
options: No way for states to send delegates
No one to enforce national laws
questions.explanation: The Articles had a Congress but no separate executive to carry out its decisions. Congress under the Articles could already declare war and make treaties.

questions.stem: The necessary and proper clause is the main basis for
options: the reserved powers of the states
questions.explanation: The clause lets Congress make laws needed to carry out its listed powers, so it can act on powers that are implied rather than spelled out.

questions.stem: A court judgment won in one state is enforced by the courts of another state because of
options: the full faith and credit clause
the necessary and proper clause of Article I
questions.explanation: Article IV requires each state to give full faith and credit to the public acts, records and court rulings of the other states.

questions.stem: Congress gives a state a lump sum for community development that it may spend as it chooses within that broad area. This is
questions.explanation: A block grant funds a broad policy area and leaves the details to the state. A categorical grant is for a narrow purpose with conditions.

questions.stem: Cooperative federalism is best described as
options: levels of government sharing policy work
the national government ruling the states
states able to nullify federal laws
the nation and states in separate spheres
questions.explanation: Under cooperative federalism the national and state governments share responsibility for policies such as highways and health care. Separate spheres describe dual federalism.

questions.stem: The Constitution's bans on ex post facto laws and bills of attainder are examples of
questions.explanation: Article I forbids Congress (and the states) to punish acts after the fact or to declare a person guilty by statute, so these protect individuals by limiting government.

questions.stem: Article V makes amending the Constitution difficult mainly to
options: keep the states out of the process
give the president a veto on amendments
let the courts approve each change first
questions.explanation: Supermajorities in Congress and the states mean only broad, lasting agreement can change the Constitution. The president and courts have no formal role, and the states have a large one.

questions.stem: The Declaration of Independence's ideas of natural rights and consent draw most directly on the work of
questions.explanation: Locke argued that people have natural rights to life, liberty and property and that government rests on their consent. Hobbes favored an all-powerful sovereign.

questions.stem: In the excerpt, "unity" refers to
options: one person holding the executive power
questions.explanation: Hamilton argues for a single executive rather than a plural one, since one person acts with more decision, secrecy and dispatch than a group.

questions.stem: Which feature of the Constitution reflects the excerpt's call for "duration"?
questions.explanation: Duration means a term long enough for the executive to act firmly; the Constitution gives the president four years with the chance of reelection.

questions.stem: An Anti-Federalist would most likely reply to the excerpt that a single executive
options: would be controlled by the courts
should be chosen by state legislatures
could grow into a kind of monarch
would be too weak to act in a crisis
questions.explanation: Anti-Federalists feared that one powerful executive with a long term and command of the army could become a king in all but name.

questions.stem: A representative polls her district and votes as most residents prefer, even against her own view. She is acting under the
questions.explanation: A delegate votes as constituents wish; a trustee uses personal judgment about their interests.

questions.stem: A member adds money for a bridge in her own district to a large spending bill. This is known as
options: a pocket veto of the bill
questions.explanation: Pork barrel spending directs federal money to a member's district or state. Logrolling is trading votes.

questions.stem: House members can force a bill out of a committee that refuses to act on it by
questions.explanation: A discharge petition signed by a majority of House members (218) brings a bill to the floor. Cloture ends debate in the Senate.

questions.stem: When the House and Senate pass different versions of a bill, the differences can be settled by
questions.explanation: A conference committee of members from both chambers writes a compromise version, which each chamber must then pass.

questions.stem: Which is an example of mandatory spending in the federal budget?
questions.explanation: Mandatory spending, such as Social Security and Medicare, is set by existing law and paid automatically. Discretionary spending, such as defense, is set each year in appropriations.

questions.stem: The custom that lets senators from a nominee's home state block a federal district judge is
questions.explanation: Through senatorial courtesy, home-state senators can stop a district court or similar nomination, usually by withholding approval on the Judiciary Committee's blue slip.

questions.stem: A president refuses to hand Congress records of private advice from aides, claiming
questions.explanation: Executive privilege is the claimed right to keep some executive communications confidential; the Court in United States v. Nixon held it is not absolute.

questions.stem: Second-term presidents often have less influence over Congress late in their terms mainly because
options: their cabinet must resign by law
questions.explanation: The Twenty-second Amendment bars a third elected term, so a second-term president becomes a lame duck as members look to the next election.

questions.stem: Under the Constitution, bills for raising revenue must start in
options: a joint committee of both houses
questions.explanation: Article I, Section 7 requires revenue bills to originate in the House, the chamber closest to the people; the Senate may amend them.

questions.stem: Which situation is an example of divided government?
options: One party holds both chambers and the presidency
One party holds the House, another the presidency
A state's two senators come from different parties
Two parties share seats on the same committee
questions.explanation: Divided government means different parties control the presidency and at least one chamber of Congress.

questions.stem: The author calls the judiciary "least dangerous" because it
options: shares its law-making power with the Senate
controls neither the money nor the army
can be overruled by the states
is chosen directly by the people
questions.explanation: Hamilton says Congress holds the purse and the president the sword, while the courts have only judgment and must rely on the other branches to enforce rulings.

questions.stem: Which feature of the Constitution does Federalist No. 78 defend to protect the independence of judges?
options: Removal by a vote of the House
questions.explanation: Hamilton defends tenure during good behavior, in effect life terms, so judges can rule against popular majorities without fear for their jobs.

questions.stem: The excerpt's claim that interpreting the laws belongs to the courts was put into practice in
questions.explanation: Marbury established judicial review, the courts' power to decide that a law conflicts with the Constitution, as Hamilton had argued.

questions.stem: A lower federal court is bound to follow
options: precedents set by the Supreme Court
the dissenting opinion in a split decision
questions.explanation: Under stare decisis and the court hierarchy, lower courts must apply the Supreme Court's precedents. Dissents carry no binding force.

questions.stem: A justice who disagrees with the majority and explains why writes
questions.explanation: A dissent explains why a justice disagrees with the ruling. A concurrence agrees with the result for different reasons.

questions.stem: A justice who agrees with the result but for different reasons writes
questions.explanation: A concurring opinion supports the outcome while giving separate reasoning.

questions.stem: An interest group that is not a party to a case files written arguments to influence the Court. This filing is
questions.explanation: An amicus curiae (friend of the court) brief lets outside groups present arguments in a case they are not party to.

questions.stem: Which is an independent regulatory agency?
options: The Office of Management and Budget
questions.explanation: Independent regulatory agencies such as the FEC are run by commissioners with fixed terms and stand outside the cabinet departments. OMB is part of the Executive Office of the President.

questions.stem: Most federal civil servants keep their jobs when a new president takes office because
options: they are hired under merit rules
the Senate confirms each of them
they are elected by the voters
questions.explanation: Most federal workers are hired and protected under civil service merit rules. Only a few thousand top posts are political appointments.

questions.stem: A president can most directly shape an agency's direction by
questions.explanation: Presidents name agency heads and other political appointees, who set priorities. Laws and budgets need Congress, and civil servants are protected by merit rules.

questions.stem: Congress's power of the purse helps it hold agencies accountable by
options: deciding how much money they get
questions.explanation: Through appropriations Congress can raise, cut or attach conditions to agency funding. Appointments are made by the president.

questions.stem: A business sues, saying an agency's new rule goes beyond what its authorizing law allows. If the court agrees, it will
options: order Congress to pass a new law
questions.explanation: Courts can strike down agency rules that exceed the authority Congress delegated, a check on the bureaucracy. Courts cannot rewrite statutes or fire officials.

questions.stem: The number of justices on the Supreme Court is set by
questions.explanation: The Constitution creates the Supreme Court but leaves its size to Congress, which has changed it several times by statute.

questions.stem: The proclamation is an example of a president acting through
questions.explanation: Lincoln issued the proclamation on his own authority as president, without a vote of Congress or an amendment.

questions.stem: Why did supporters of emancipation still push for a constitutional amendment after the proclamation?
options: The proclamation had applied only to free states
The Supreme Court had struck it down
A wartime order could be challenged or undone
questions.explanation: An order resting on wartime power could be questioned in court or reversed later; an amendment would end slavery permanently and everywhere.

questions.stem: The course pairs the proclamation with later civil rights decisions as examples of
options: the courts limiting the war powers
states gaining power over the national government
government acting to protect minority rights
questions.explanation: The framework lists the proclamation, followed by the Thirteenth Amendment, among the times government protected rather than restricted minority rights.

questions.stem: A government order that blocks a story before it is published is called
questions.explanation: Prior restraint is censorship in advance of publication, which the Court presumes unconstitutional. Libel is a false written statement that harms a reputation.

questions.stem: Burning a flag as a political protest is protected as
questions.explanation: The Court treats expressive conduct such as flag burning or wearing armbands as symbolic speech under the First Amendment.

questions.stem: A state pays the salaries of teachers at the schools of only one religion. This most likely violates
questions.explanation: Government funding that favors or supports one religion runs against the establishment clause's bar on government establishment of religion.

questions.stem: A defendant held for years while prosecutors delay her trial without reason could claim a violation of the
questions.explanation: The Sixth Amendment guarantees a speedy and public trial in criminal cases. The Seventh concerns juries in civil suits.

questions.stem: After a jury acquits a defendant, the state cannot try her again for the same crime because of
options: the right to a speedy trial
questions.explanation: The Fifth Amendment says no one may be twice put in jeopardy for the same offense.

questions.stem: Which is best described as a civil right rather than a civil liberty?
options: Freedom to worship as one chooses
questions.explanation: Civil rights are protections against discrimination, such as equal treatment. Civil liberties are freedoms protected from government interference.

questions.stem: Brown v. Board of Education (1954) and Shaw v. Reno (1993) were both decided under
questions.explanation: Brown held that race-based school segregation violates equal protection, and Shaw that a district drawn only by race can be challenged under the same clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

questions.stem: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 attacked racial discrimination in voting mainly by
options: ending poll taxes in all federal elections
offering registration at motor vehicle offices
suspending literacy tests and adding federal oversight
questions.explanation: The act suspended literacy tests and put federal examiners and federal review of election-law changes in places with a history of discrimination. The Twenty-fourth Amendment ended poll taxes in federal elections, the Twenty-sixth lowered the voting age, and the 1993 motor voter law added registration at motor vehicle offices.

questions.stem: The Court has applied most of the Bill of Rights to the states through the due process clause of the
questions.explanation: The Fourteenth Amendment says no state may deprive a person of liberty without due process of law. The Fifth Amendment's due process clause limits the federal government.

questions.stem: After an attack, Congress widens government collection of phone records. Critics would most likely argue that this threatens
options: the Second Amendment right to bear arms
the Sixth Amendment right to counsel
the powers reserved to the states
questions.explanation: Surveillance raises the question of balancing national security against the Fourth Amendment's protection from unreasonable searches and seizures.

questions.stem: Smith's main point in the excerpt is that
options: merchants should act out of charity
self-interest in markets meets people's needs
trade should stay inside each town and its own market
government must set the price of food
questions.explanation: Smith argues that we get our dinner because sellers profit from selling it, so self-interest, not kindness, supplies people's wants through exchange.

questions.stem: Which core value in the course is most closely tied to Smith's ideas?
questions.explanation: The course describes free enterprise as the pursuit of self-interest, competition and limited regulation of the market, as espoused by Adam Smith.

questions.stem: A policymaker who draws on Smith's ideas would most likely favor
questions.explanation: Smith argued that competition guided by self-interest allocates resources well and opposed most trade barriers, so his followers favor light regulation.

questions.stem: Which policy best reflects the value of equality of opportunity?
options: Free public schools open to all
Equal incomes for every family in the country
questions.explanation: Equality of opportunity means everyone gets an equal chance to compete, as free public education aims to give; equal incomes would be equality of outcome.

questions.stem: A liberal is more likely than a conservative to support
options: lower tax rates on the very highest incomes
questions.explanation: Liberals generally favor a larger government role in regulating the economy and providing services. The other three are conservative positions.

questions.stem: A major event shapes the political views of an entire age group for the rest of their lives. This is
questions.explanation: A generational effect comes from shared formative experiences, such as a war or depression, during youth. A life-cycle effect is change as people age.

questions.stem: A sharp but short rise in public approval of the president after a foreign attack is
questions.explanation: In a crisis, Americans often unite behind the president for a time, so approval jumps and then fades.

questions.stem: Increasing a poll's random sample from 400 to 1,600 people would most likely
options: remove every source of sampling bias
questions.explanation: Sampling error falls as a random sample grows: quadrupling the sample roughly halves the margin of error. A larger sample does not fix bias or wording.

questions.stem: An online poll that anyone can join is less reliable mainly because
options: its questions are too short to answer well
questions.explanation: Self-selected samples draw people with strong feelings or interest, so they do not represent the population.

questions.stem: Members of the Federal Reserve Board serve long, staggered terms so that
options: it is shielded from short-term politics
Congress can set interest rates every day
questions.explanation: Long terms give the Fed independence, so monetary policy is set without pressure from each election cycle.

questions.stem: Cutting tax rates to encourage investment and work, expecting growth to follow, is
questions.explanation: Supply-side economics holds that lower taxes and less regulation raise production and growth.

questions.stem: People who get news mostly from feeds that match their own views may grow more polarized because of
questions.explanation: Echo chambers repeat and reinforce what people already believe, so opposing views rarely reach them.

questions.stem: A conservative is more likely than a liberal to support
options: higher taxes on the very top incomes
questions.explanation: Conservatives generally oppose new limits on gun ownership and favor lower taxes and less regulation; the other three are liberal positions.

questions.stem: Turnout among people with a bachelor's degree or more is how many percentage points higher than among people without a high school diploma?
questions.explanation: 77 - 35 = 42 points. 25 compares the degree group with diploma holders (77 - 52), and 17 compares diploma holders with those without one.

questions.stem: Which statement is best supported by the table?
options: Education has no link to turnout
Most people without a diploma vote
questions.explanation: Turnout climbs at every step, from 35% without a diploma to 77% with a degree.

questions.stem: Which explanation of the pattern fits political science research best?
options: Ballots are printed only for graduates
Only graduates may register to vote
Graduates live in states with more elections
questions.explanation: Education builds knowledge, skills and a sense that one's vote matters (efficacy), all linked to higher turnout. No law limits voting by education.

questions.stem: A citizen who believes her vote can change government policy has high
questions.explanation: Political efficacy is the belief that one can understand and influence politics; people with high efficacy vote more.

questions.stem: Which is a main function of political parties?
options: Counting the electoral votes each January
questions.explanation: Parties recruit candidates, nominate them, mobilize voters and organize government. Agencies write regulations and the Senate confirms judges.

questions.stem: A lasting shift in which groups support each party, often marked by one election, is
questions.explanation: In a critical election and realignment, new coalitions form and last for years. Dealignment is a weakening of party ties without a new alignment.

questions.stem: Third parties most often affect American politics by
options: winning control of several state legislatures
pushing major parties to adopt their ideas
questions.explanation: When a third party's issue draws votes, a major party often takes up the issue to win those voters back.

questions.stem: A voter chooses a Republican for president and a Democrat for the House. This is
questions.explanation: Ticket splitting is voting for candidates of different parties for different offices on the same ballot.

questions.stem: A closed primary is one in which
options: only registered party members may vote
any registered voter may take part
the top two finishers always advance
questions.explanation: Closed primaries limit voting to the party's registered members. Open primaries let voters choose a party's ballot on the day.

questions.stem: Which is a structural barrier to voting?
questions.explanation: Structural barriers are rules and procedures, such as registration deadlines, that make voting harder. The others are attitudes.

questions.stem: Turnout in the United States is lower than in some democracies partly because some of those countries
options: elect far more officials each year
questions.explanation: Compulsory voting, as in Australia, pushes turnout far higher. Electing more officials more often tends to lower turnout through voter fatigue.

questions.stem: A party's formal statement of its positions, adopted at its national convention, is its
questions.explanation: The platform sets out the party's positions on issues; individual planks address specific policies.

questions.stem: Under proportional representation, a party winning 20 percent of the vote would usually get
options: about a fifth of the seats
a single seat for the whole party
half the seats in the legislature
no seats unless it came first
questions.explanation: Proportional systems give parties seats in rough proportion to their vote share, which helps smaller parties win seats.

questions.stem: The memo best illustrates
options: the use of data to target voters
questions.explanation: The campaign matches voter files with consumer data to send different messages to different households, a hallmark of modern campaigns.

questions.stem: Which change in modern campaigns does the memo reflect?
options: Candidate-centered campaigns with their own staff
Campaigns paid for only with public funds
Party machines running the campaigns of candidates
Candidates relying on newspapers to reach voters
questions.explanation: The campaign has its own data team and donors and says it will not depend on the state party, showing how campaigns center on candidates and professional consultants.

questions.stem: The memo's reliance on small online donations reflects which development?
options: A ban on all contributions from individuals
Raising money from many supporters online
Federal limits on large donations ending
Parties paying for most House races
questions.explanation: The internet lets campaigns collect many small gifts cheaply, so a candidate can fund a race from a broad base of supporters.

questions.stem: A super PAC may
options: coordinate ads with a candidate's staff
spend without limit but not coordinate
give unlimited sums directly to candidates
questions.explanation: Super PACs may raise and spend unlimited sums on independent expenditures but may not give directly to or coordinate with candidates.

questions.stem: The Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act of 2002 mainly targeted
options: limits on lobbying by former members
soft money given to the parties
questions.explanation: The act, also called McCain-Feingold, banned national parties from raising unlimited soft money and regulated issue ads near elections.

questions.stem: Parties, interest groups, elections and the media are called linkage institutions because they
options: connect the states to each other
join the House and Senate in conference
questions.explanation: Linkage institutions are channels through which people's concerns become political issues on the government's agenda.

questions.stem: When heavy news coverage leads the public to see an issue as important, the media is
questions.explanation: Agenda setting is the media's influence on which issues the public and officials think matter most.

questions.stem: Reporters uncover misuse of funds by a city agency. The media is acting as
questions.explanation: As a watchdog, the press investigates officials and exposes wrongdoing. As a scorekeeper it tracks who is winning politically.

questions.stem: Each state's number of electoral votes equals
options: its population divided by one million
its House seats plus its two senators
questions.explanation: Article II gives each state as many electors as it has senators and representatives in Congress.

questions.stem: Which advantage most helps House incumbents win reelection?
questions.explanation: Helping constituents with problems involving federal agencies builds goodwill and name recognition that challengers lack.

questions.stem: A group that works on only one issue, such as expanding or limiting gun rights, is
questions.explanation: Single-issue groups focus narrowly on one policy and often judge candidates by that issue alone.

questions.stem: An interest group urges its members to call their senators before a key vote. This is
questions.explanation: Grassroots lobbying mobilizes ordinary members to contact officials. Direct lobbying is the group's own lobbyists meeting officials.

questions.stem: The Court has allowed limits on how much a person may give directly to a candidate, while Citizens United struck limits on independent spending. The difference rests on
options: the size of the candidate's district
the Court's view that money is not speech
a ban on speech by individuals
the risk of corruption from direct gifts
questions.explanation: The Court treats direct contributions as carrying a risk of corruption or its appearance, which justifies limits; it found that independent spending does not, and treats both as forms of speech.
